newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia industry chief calls for GST.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia industry chief calls for GST.

text.p: Australian Industry Commission chairman Bill Scales called on Wednesday for the introduction of a consumption tax and definition of indigenous land title, calling them two major economic priorities.
In an aggressive speech to a business breakfast in Melbourne, Scales rejected suggestions that Australia should not proceed unilaterally to slash import tarrifs.
"To wait for others (to cut tarrifs) is tantamount to giving other countries veto over Australia's trade policy," Scales said.
"I hope to this audience that it is self evident that this is naive in the extreme and particularly self defeating."
Scales also called for fundamental change to Australia's tax system.

"The Commission sees the introduction of a broad based consumption tax as a realistic long tern goal," Scales said. Prime Minister John Howard's Coalition government has ruled out introducing of a goods and service tax (GST) in its first term in office.
On the issue of indigenous land title, Scales said legal uncertainties over the concept affected a corner stone of Australia's economy - property rights.
"Clear and unambiguous understanding of property rights is a corner stone of economic progress in a free enterprise economy," he said.

"Resolving this complex issue of native title in general, and the Wik decision in particular, is important both now and in the future. The longer that these issues remain unclear, the longer they will be likely to delay important investment decisions," Scales said.

In December the High Court, Australia's supreme tribunal, ruled that traditional Aboriginal ownership of land, which it had invented in 1992, existed even when a state government had leased the land to pastoralists.

In the Wik case, named after the Wik aboriginal people, who were litigants, the court ruled that leases and the native title existed together, giving aborigines some kind of right to access and, when the leases expired, full ownership.
The exact rights of the Aborigines are unclear, and primary producers and some states have said the resulting uncertainty is enough to discourage investment.
